content: Micronutrient deficiencies are frequently observed in adults living with HIV, particularly in low-income regions where diets often lack essential vitamins and minerals. Certain micronutrients play vital roles in supporting the immune system, and regular supplementation has been proposed as a potential strategy to improve health outcomes in this population. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of micronutrient supplementation in reducing mortality and HIV-related complications in HIV-positive adults, excluding pregnant women. To achieve this, a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted, including studies published between January 2010 and November 2016. The databases searched included CENTRAL, Embase, and PubMed, along with trial registries such as the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov. The review included 33 trials with a total of 10,325 participants, of which 17 were newly identified studies. The trials compared single, dual, or multiple micronutrient supplements to placebo, no treatment, or other supplements. Studies focusing on micronutrient use for managing metabolic complications related to antiretroviral therapy (ART) were excluded. The primary outcomes assessed were all-cause mortality, morbidity, and disease progression. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR), hazard ratios (HR), and mean differences (MD), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Findings on Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation: 1. Mortality: Routine supplementation with multiple micronutrients appeared to have little or no effect on mortality in adults living with HIV (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.15; 7 trials, 2897 participants; low-certainty evidence). 2. CD4+ Cell Count: Over a period of up to two years, supplementation had little or no effect on the average CD4+ cell count (MD 26.40 cells/mm³, 95% CI −22.91 to 75.70; 6 trials, 1581 participants; low-certainty evidence). 3. Viral Load: There was little or no effect on the average viral load (MD −0.1 log10 viral copies, 95% CI −0.26 to 0.06; 4 trials, 840 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). 4. Specific Findings: One trial in ART-naïve adults in Botswana reported a delay in the time to reach a CD4+ cell count below 250 cells/mm³ after two years of high-dose supplementation (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.88; 1 trial, 439 participants). However, this effect was observed only in the group receiving multiple micronutrients combined with selenium, and the findings were inconsistent with other trials using similar combinations. 5. Adverse Events: In one trial comparing high-dose versus standard-dose supplementation in individuals on ART, high-dose supplementation was associated with a lower incidence of peripheral neuropathy (IRR 0.81, 95% CI 0.7 to 0.94; 1 trial, 3418 participants). However, the trial was terminated early due to increased adverse events, including elevated alanine transaminase (ALT) levels, in the high-dose group. Findings on Single or Dual Micronutrient Supplementation: 1. Mortality and Morbidity: None of the trials were adequately powered to detect significant effects on mortality or morbidity outcomes. 2. CD4+ Cell Count and Viral Load: No clinically meaningful changes in CD4+ cell count (14 trials, 2370 participants; very low or low-certainty evidence) or viral load (7 studies, 1334 participants; very low or low-certainty evidence) were reported. 3. Micronutrient Levels: Supplementation likely increased blood concentrations of vitamin D and zinc (vitamin D: 4 trials, 299 participants; zinc: 4 trials, 484 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and may have increased vitamin A levels (3 trials, 495 participants; low-certainty evidence), particularly in individuals with pre-existing deficiencies. Conclusions: The available evidence does not consistently demonstrate clinically significant benefits of routine multiple micronutrient supplementation in adults living with HIV. While larger trials may uncover small but meaningful effects, the current findings should not discourage the use of micronutrient supplements in cases where specific deficiencies are identified or where dietary intake is insufficient to meet recommended daily allowances.
